newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Bolger likely to remain as PM - ACT's Prebble.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Bolger likely to remain as PM - ACT's Prebble.

text.p: ACT New Zealand leader Richard Prebble on Sunday backed Prime Minister Jim Bolger to hang onto the country's top job following an historic but inconclusive general election.

"He's the prime minister. We're going to see Jim Bolger going on being prime minister and I think he might go on being prime minister for quite a long time, maybe the whole three years," Prebble told Radio New Zealand.
Prebble's radical free-market party won eight seats in Saturday's poll, the first under the new Mixed Member Proportional system of representation.
He said ACT was committed to safeguarding the fundamental elements of National's economic direction.
"We are in favour of the Reserve Bank Act, the Fiscal Responsibilty Act, the Employment Contracts Act and the liberalisation of the economy," Prebble said.
But that support alone will not be enough to return Bolger and his ministers to the government benches.
Economic nationalist New Zealand First holds the balance of power after results gave it 17 seats, the conservative National Party 44 seats and Labour 37 in a new 120-member parliament.
The left-wing Alliance, with 13 seats, has said it will not enter into a coalition, but is likely to support Labour on social policy issues.
Bolger and Labour leader Helen Clark have each said they aim to lead the next government, but both need the support of New Zealand First, which has not said which way it will lean.

Prebble said Bolger would only stop being prime minister if a majority of the members of parliament decided to bring him down. "And at the moment, New Zealand First has said that it won't do that," he said.
Prebble said the election outcome clearly showed a swing away from the left and predicted that the right would prevail.
"The centre-right went up in the election campaign and the centre-left went down. Not only did Labour take a big hit, but so did the Alliance," he said.

"Put is this way: Labour was saying 'we're going to wander in and be a minority government'. No they aren't! The only way they can do that is to pursuade a majority of MPs to vote for the party that had a huge swing against them."
Prebble said professional politicians would look at the vote and say "Heck, Jim Bolger managed to get almost the same vote as he got last election, and governments normally erode."
